I'll let Claude handle this: "Product liability is decent at exactly the AI harms that worry people least, and structurally unfit for the ones that worry people most. The clean way to see it is to write down what product liability quietly assumes, then check which assumptions advanced AI violates.

Product liability works when: (1) a product is placed in commerce, (2) it causes a bounded, ex-post-remediable harm, (3) to an identifiable plaintiff, (4) through a short causal chain without intervening criminal acts, (5) where a reasonable alternative design existed and the defect was knowable, and (6) the defendant can actually pay. Mundane AI harms—hallucinated defamation, bad medical advice, discriminatory lending, a chatbot that encourages self-harm—satisfy most of these, and liability plus the insurance market it spawns will probably handle them about as well as it handled cars and pharma. That's a real point in Huang's favor, and I'd push back on treating the whole position as obviously wrong.

Where it breaks, roughly in order of how much it matters:

Judgment-proof tails. Liability deters by making expected damages exceed expected gains. Once potential harm exceeds a firm's assets—bio uplift, critical infrastructure, a cascading financial event—the marginal deterrent goes to zero, because limited liability truncates the downside at bankruptcy. This is the textbook case for ex ante regulation and why nuclear power got Price-Anderson rather than tort law. The "bad model" framing implicitly assumes harms are on the compensable part of the curve.

Intervening misuse. The characteristic frontier-model risk is uplift: the model makes a human attacker more capable. Tort doctrine has spent a century cutting liability off at the intervening criminal act (firearms, platforms via Section 230, the "learned intermediary"). Open-weight releases make this worse—the chain runs model → fine-tuner → deployer → user → victim, and courts tend to assign fault to the last human. So liability is weakest precisely on the misuse vector.

Knowability and the standard of care. "Don't release bad models" presumes badness is detectable pre-release. Design-defect claims need a reasonable alternative design and foreseeability; negligence is benchmarked to industry custom. If every lab ships with the same eval suite and something emergent gets through, nobody was negligent by the industry's own standard—and the industry sets that standard. The whole safety worry is about latent capabilities and behaviors evals miss, which is exactly the case where "you should have known" is hardest to prove.

No product, no plaintiff. Liability requires a product in commerce and a victim with standing. Pre-release risks—internal deployment for automated AI R&D, weight theft by a state actor, a model exfiltrating itself—involve no product and no consumer. Diffuse harms—labor displacement, epistemic degradation, concentration of power—have no plaintiff at all. These aren't edge cases; they're most of the "advanced AI" part of advanced AI risk.

Latency and correlation. Asbestos litigation eventually produced enormous damages and compensated almost nobody adequately, decades late. Slow or cumulative harms get litigated after the fact, and correlated catastrophic risk is precisely the kind insurers refuse to underwrite (see terrorism and flood), so the insurance-as-private-regulator mechanism that makes liability work elsewhere may not form.

Race dynamics. A firm facing a tiny probability of an unpayable loss against a large probability of enormous upside will rationally accept the bet, especially if competitors are taking it too. Liability regimes assume defendants' incentives are roughly aligned with social cost; here the misalignment is built into the cap."

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

WHEN A COURT ORDER HAS TO BE CORRECTED — QUESTIONS OF JUDICIAL TRANSPARENCY

The video claims that the Supreme Court had to reconsider its order in the Medha Roopam–Akriti Chaudhary NSA detention case, amid public and legal questions over the manner in which the matter was listed and heard. 

The documented sequence is important.

On 23 September 2026, the Supreme Court initially stayed the Allahabad High Court judgment in the case. The matter was heard by Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and N. Kotiswar Singh, and the proceedings were conducted with the audio muted. 

On 24 September, the Supreme Court modified/clarified its order. The stay was confined to the High Court's adverse strictures and its direction concerning ₹5 lakh compensation. The High Court's decision quashing Akriti Chaudhary's NSA detention remained operative. 

There is also a separate issue concerning the roster. Legal reporting has noted that the bench hearing the matter did not ordinarily have the roster for preventive-detention matters under the roster then in force, while related proceedings were pending before a bench headed by Justice B.V. Nagarathna. 

That does not, by itself, establish wrongdoing. But it raises a legitimate institutional question:

When judicial power affects personal liberty, can transparency about listing, roster allocation and proceedings ever be treated as a secondary matter?

Democracy does not require citizens to distrust courts.
It requires institutions powerful enough to decide citizens' liberty to remain open to scrutiny, reasoned explanation and accountability.

The issue is not who wins a particular case.
The issue is whether every citizen can see that justice is being administered by transparent and consistent rules.

Can the Government suspend a political party’s Instagram handle without a clear statutory power? And can a politician boycott a courtroom while simultaneously asking the Supreme Court to transfer the same judge from hearing his case?  

This week, the Aam Aadmi Party raised both questions in two different constitutional courtrooms.  

In the Supreme Court, AAP challenged the suspension of its Gujarat unit’s Instagram handle, arguing that Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act was never meant to become a direct content-blocking weapon. 

Senior Advocate Shadan Farasat argued that the provision only deals with “safe harbour” obligations of intermediaries — not independent censorship powers.  The party says the move violates Article 19(1)(a), the constitutional guarantee of free speech. 

The Supreme Court has now issued notice to the Centre.  At the same time in the Delhi High Court, Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma appointed three amicus curiae for Arvind Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia, and Satyendar Jain after the leaders chose to boycott proceedings, invoking “Mahatma Gandhi’s Satyagraha principles” and claiming their faith in the court process had been shaken.  

But here’s the constitutional twist: Kejriwal had also moved the Supreme Court seeking transfer of the excise policy case away from Justice Sharma’s bench — even as his legal team withdrew from participation before her court.  

This has now created a rare constitutional confrontation involving: 
⚖️ Article 19 vs state regulation of digital speech 
⚖️ Article 21 vs procedural fairness in criminal prosecution 
⚖️ Judicial recusal vs courtroom boycott 
⚖️ Free speech, due process, and strategic constitutional litigation  Justice Sharma’s response may become one of the most significant procedural moments in the case: instead of proceeding ex parte, she chose to appoint independent senior advocates as amicus curiae to preserve procedural fairness.  

And one line from the Supreme Court hearing may define this entire battle: “Today my portal is gone.”  Because this is no longer just about an Instagram account.

 It is about whether opposition parties in India can lose their digital voice overnight — and what constitutional remedy exists when that happens.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

You are building workflows and calling them agents

And until you see the difference, your agents will keep breaking over and over again

Three levels, each for a different job.

A model. For anything where every fact is already in your message: drafting, rewriting, explaining. Nothing to set up. If the answer needs something it cannot see, paste that thing in.

A workflow. For a job with the same shape every time. Write the trigger, the steps in order, and which tool does each step. 

Have every step output fixed fields instead of prose, so the next step can read it, and keep a log of each run so you know which step broke. Run it by hand five times before you put it on a schedule.

An agent. For when the number of steps depends on the input. Write the goal and what done means, describe the tools well enough that it can pick between them, give it a way to check its own output, and cap the turns before you walk away.

The question was never how smart the model is. It is who picked the order of the steps.

IT'S KNOWING WHAT DESERVES A SECOND LOOK.

A message arrives.

A payment request changes.

A headline explodes.

A seller makes a claim.

A recruiter contacts you.

A link looks slightly strange.

A price seems incredible.

An AI gives you an answer.

A document contains an important number.

A company makes a promise.

A video goes viral.

Your instinct says:

“I GOTTA CHECK THAT.”

That tiny moment—

between seeing something and trusting it—

could become an enormous product category.

Because the modern internet increasingly asks humans to make decisions inside an environment filled with:

AI-generated content.

Impersonation.

Phishing.

Fake reviews.

Synthetic media.

Misleading claims.

Manipulated screenshots.

Fraudulent sellers.

Copied websites.

Questionable statistics.

Outdated information.

And perfectly legitimate information that simply lacks:

CONTEXT.

So here's the opportunity:

WHAT IF “CHECK THIS” BECAME A UNIVERSAL ACTION ACROSS THE INTERNET?

That's the company hiding inside:

https://t.co/FXdzztKY9O

I wouldn't build another search engine.

I wouldn't build another simplistic “true / false” fact-checking site.

And I wouldn't build an AI that pretends certainty where evidence doesn't exist.

I'd build:

THE UNIVERSAL VERIFICATION + TRUST INTELLIGENCE LAYER FOR THE INTERNET.

One architecture:

THING → CLAIM → SOURCE → IDENTITY → EVIDENCE → CONTEXT → RISK → CHECK → EXPLANATION → DECISION → MEMORY

One principle:

BEFORE YOU TRUST IT. GOTTA CHECK.™

🔥🔥🔥

🔎 GOTTA CHECK™

See something questionable?

Send it to GottaCheck.

Link.

Screenshot.

Email.

Text.

Image.

Video.

Product.

Seller.

Company.

Profile.

Document.

Claim.

Phone number.

QR code.

AI answer.

Then ask:

WHAT AM I LOOKING AT — AND WHAT SHOULD I VERIFY?

🔥🔥🔥

⚡ CHECK THIS™

The universal action.

Share something into GottaCheck.

The system identifies:

What it is.

What it claims.

Who appears to be behind it.

What evidence exists.

What deserves attention.

Instead of requiring the user to become:

AN INTERNET DETECTIVE.

🔥🔥🔥

🧠 CHECK AI™

AI doesn't simply answer:

Safe.

or:

Fake.

It investigates.

Break the object into:

Claims.

Entities.

Sources.

Dates.

Links.

Identities.

Documents.

Images.

Contradictions.

Risk signals.

Then explain:

WHAT WE KNOW, WHAT WE DON'T, AND WHAT YOU SHOULD CHECK NEXT.

🔥🔥🔥

🧩 CLAIM SPLIT™

One paragraph may contain:

Five factual claims.

Three opinions.

One prediction.

Two numbers.

Separate them.

Because:

ONE BAD CLAIM SHOULDN'T CONTAMINATE AN ENTIRE DOCUMENT — AND ONE TRUE CLAIM SHOULDN'T VALIDATE EVERYTHING ELSE.

🔥🔥🔥

📚 SOURCE STACK™

Where did the information originate?

Original source?

News article?

Press release?

Research paper?

Government record?

Social post?

Anonymous screenshot?

AI-generated summary?

Build:

THE SOURCE CHAIN.

🔥🔥🔥

🎯 ORIGINAL SOURCE™

A thousand websites repeat the same claim.

That doesn't create:

A THOUSAND SOURCES.

Find where it began.

Then show:

Who said it.

When.

In what context.

And whether the repeated versions changed:

THE ORIGINAL MEANING.

🔥🔥🔥

🧬 SOURCE DNA™

Analyze the source itself.

Domain.

Publisher.

Author.

Date.

Ownership where available.

Citation behavior.

Historical context.

Known impersonation signals.

The question isn't only:

WHAT DOES THIS PAGE SAY?

It's:

WHERE DID THIS COME FROM?

🔥🔥🔥

🗓️ DATE CHECK™

Old information can become misinformation simply by being:

REPOSTED AS NEW.

Check:

Original publication.

Updates.

Referenced period.

Event date.

Screenshot date.

Because context changes.

🔥🔥🔥

🔢 NUMBER CHECK™

Someone says:

“Sales increased 300%.”

GottaCheck asks:

From what baseline?

Over what period?

Which population?

Nominal or real?

Absolute or relative?

Numbers deserve:

CONTEXT — NOT JUST CONFIDENCE.

🔥🔥🔥

💬 QUOTE CHECK™

Viral quote.

Did the person actually say it?

Where?

When?

Full sentence?

Edited clip?

Different context?

Translation?

Find:

THE ORIGINAL RECORD.

🔥🔥🔥

📊 CHART CHECK™

Charts can be technically accurate and still mislead.

Check:

Axis.

Scale.

Time period.

Missing data.

Population.

Source.

Normalization.

The graph isn't automatically:

THE EVIDENCE.

🔥🔥🔥

🖼️ IMAGE CHECK™

Upload an image.

Look for:

Source clues.

Earlier appearances.

Possible manipulation.

Context mismatch.

Synthetic-generation indicators where detectable.

But avoid pretending detection is perfect.

The output should communicate:

EVIDENCE + UNCERTAINTY.

🔥🔥🔥

🎥 VIDEO CHECK™

A clip goes viral.

Check:

Original upload.

Longer version.

Date.

Location.

Sequence.

Audio context.

Known edits.

Related reporting.

Because 12 seconds can completely change:

A 12-MINUTE EVENT.

🔥🔥🔥

✂️ CLIP CONTEXT™

Show:

Before.

Clip.

After.

A powerful verification product doesn't merely inspect media.

It restores:

THE MISSING CONTEXT.

🔥🔥🔥

🤖 AI CHECK™

Paste an AI answer.

GottaCheck identifies:

Factual assertions.

Citations.

Numbers.

Names.

Dates.

Then verifies what can actually be verified.

AI-generated confidence becomes:

A STARTING POINT — NOT PROOF.

🔥🔥🔥

📎 CITATION CHECK™

AI gives five citations.

Do they exist?

Do they support the claim?

Are they primary?

Are they current?

Are they being represented accurately?

One click:

CHECK THE SOURCES BEHIND THE ANSWER.

🔥🔥🔥

🧠 CONFIDENCE GAP™

AI sounds:

95% certain.

Evidence supports:

Much less.

GottaCheck can expose the gap between:

HOW CONFIDENT SOMETHING SOUNDS

and:

HOW STRONG THE EVIDENCE ACTUALLY IS.

🔥🔥🔥

📧 EMAIL CHECK™

Suspicious email?

Forward it.

Analyze:

Sender.

Domain.

Reply-to.

Links.

Language.

Requested action.

Payment changes.

Impersonation clues.

The question becomes:

SHOULD I TRUST THIS MESSAGE ENOUGH TO ACT?

🔥🔥🔥

💸 PAYMENT CHANGE™

Email says:

We've changed our banking information.

That deserves more than:

A QUICK GLANCE.

GottaCheck can flag:

New payment destination.

Sender changes.

Domain differences.

Urgency.

Unusual language.

Then recommend:

VERIFY THROUGH A KNOWN, INDEPENDENT CHANNEL BEFORE SENDING MONEY.

🔥🔥🔥

🔗 LINK CHECK™

Paste a link before opening it.

Inspect:

Domain.

Redirect chain.

Lookalike spelling.

HTTPS.

Destination.

Reputation signals.

Page age where available.

Potential impersonation.

One habit:

LINK LOOKS WEIRD? GOTTA CHECK.

🔥🔥🔥

🌐 DOMAIN CHECK™

Is this really:

The bank?

The retailer?

The government service?

The delivery company?

Or a lookalike?

Compare:

Domain structure.

Official references.

Brand identity.

Known domains.

Registration context where useful.

Because one character can separate:

LEGITIMATE FROM FRAUDULENT.

🔥🔥🔥

📱 QR CHECK™

Scan a QR code.

Before opening:

Show destination.

Redirects.

Domain.

Risk indicators.

Because QR codes hide:

WHERE YOU'RE ACTUALLY GOING.

🔥🔥🔥

📞 PHONE CHECK™

Unknown caller?

Search available public context.

Business identity.

Reported scam patterns.

Country.

Number format.

But clearly distinguish:

VERIFIED IDENTITY FROM COMMUNITY REPORTS.

🔥🔥🔥

👤 PROFILE CHECK™

Someone contacts you.

Recruiter.

Investor.

Supplier.

Customer.

Dating profile.

Professional.

Check available public evidence for:

Identity consistency.

Organization.

Domain.

Public history.

Impersonation signals.

Not:

“THIS PERSON IS FAKE.”

Instead:

HERE'S WHAT CAN — AND CANNOT — BE VERIFIED.

🔥🔥🔥

🏢 COMPANY CHECK™

Before:

Paying.

Investing.

Signing.

Ordering.

Partnering.

Check:

Corporate identity.

Website.

Domain.

Public records where available.

Leadership claims.

Contact consistency.

Warnings.

The goal:

BETTER DUE DILIGENCE BEFORE THE CLICK.

🔥🔥🔥

🛒 SELLER CHECK™

Marketplace seller looks legitimate.

Check:

Identity signals.

Store history.

Domain.

Reviews.

Product images.

Policies.

External references.

GottaCheck can help surface:

WHAT DESERVES EXTRA VERIFICATION BEFORE PURCHASE.

🔥🔥🔥

⭐ REVIEW CHECK™

Reviews influence billions in commerce.

But are they:

Organic?

Copied?

Coordinated?

AI-generated?

Incentivized?

Suspiciously repetitive?

Analyze patterns without pretending any single signal proves fraud.

SHOW THE PATTERN.

🔥🔥🔥

🛍️ PRODUCT CHECK™

Product claims:

Clinically proven.

Made locally.

Official.

Authentic.

Lifetime warranty.

Independent testing.

GottaCheck extracts:

THE CHECKABLE CLAIMS.

Then finds evidence.

🔥🔥🔥

💼 JOB CHECK™

Amazing remote job.

Huge salary.

Immediate offer.

Recruiter asks for:

Personal information.

Equipment payment.

Crypto.

Bank details.

GottaCheck examines:

Company.

Recruiter identity.

Email domain.

Job listing.

Public presence.

Requested actions.

Before someone sends:

THEIR MONEY OR IDENTITY.

Below-market price.

Owner overseas.

Deposit required immediately.

Listing duplication.

Images.

Property context.

Contact information.

Payment request.

CHECKING.

🚗 VEHICLE CHECK™

Listing.

Seller.

Photos.

Pricing anomalies.

History sources.

Payment instructions.

GottaCheck becomes:

THE SECOND LOOK BEFORE THE PURCHASE.

🔥🔥🔥

💰 INVESTMENT CLAIM™

“Guaranteed return.”

“Zero risk.”

“Exclusive opportunity.”

“Act today.”

GottaCheck identifies:

Promised returns.

Named entities.

Registration claims.

Evidence.

Warnings.

And one principle remains absolute:

NO LEGITIMATE CHECK CAN TURN RISK INTO A GUARANTEE.

🔥🔥🔥

🪙 CRYPTO CHECK™

Token.

Wallet request.

Exchange.

Project.

Airdrop.

Contract address.

Website.

Founder claim.

Check available evidence before:

CONNECTING OR SENDING.

🔥🔥🔥

📰 HEADLINE CHECK™

Headline says something explosive.

Open the article.

Extract the underlying claim.

Compare:

Headline.

Body.

Primary source.

Sometimes the first thing worth checking is:

WHETHER THE ARTICLE ACTUALLY SAYS WHAT THE HEADLINE IMPLIES.

🔥🔥🔥

🧪 STUDY CHECK™

“Scientists prove…”

Which study?

Peer reviewed?

Sample size?

Human or animal?

Observational or randomized?

Effect size?

Limitations?

Replicated?

GottaCheck translates:

RESEARCH CLAIM → ACTUAL EVIDENCE.

🔥🔥🔥

📄 DOCUMENT CHECK™

Contract.

Invoice.

Report.

Proposal.

Research.

Policy.

Upload it.

Extract:

Claims.

Dates.

Numbers.

Entities.

References.

Potential inconsistencies.

Then build:

A CHECKLIST OF WHAT DESERVES VERIFICATION.

🔥🔥🔥

🧾 INVOICE CHECK™

Vendor invoice arrives.

Compare:

Vendor identity.

Known payment information.

Amount.

Purchase order.

Historical pattern.

Banking changes.

Duplicate invoice signals.

One suspicious invoice can cost more than:

YEARS OF SOFTWARE.

🔥🔥🔥

🏷️ PRICE CHECK™

Is this actually:

A deal?

Compare available pricing context.

Historical price where available.

Other sellers.

Shipping.

Fees.

Product version.

The word:

“SALE”

isn't evidence.

🔥🔥🔥

🧑‍⚕️ HEALTH CLAIM CHECK™

Health misinformation deserves additional caution.

Identify:

Claim.

Source.

Evidence quality.

Relevant medical guidance.

Limitations.

And direct consequential personal medical decisions toward:

QUALIFIED PROFESSIONAL CARE.

GottaCheck should inform—

not impersonate:

A DOCTOR.

🔥🔥🔥

⚖️ LEGAL CLAIM CHECK™

“This is illegal.”

“You're legally required to…”

“There's a new law…”

Check:

Jurisdiction.

Actual legislation.

Effective date.

Official source.

But consequential legal decisions remain:

A JOB FOR QUALIFIED COUNSEL.

🔥🔥🔥

🏛️ PUBLIC CLAIM CHECK™

For claims involving public policy, elections or government:

Show:

Original source.

Official records.

Relevant data.

Credible reporting.

Material disagreements.

Avoid telling users:

WHAT POLITICAL CONCLUSION TO REACH.

The product verifies evidence.

The human decides.

🔥🔥🔥

📍 LOCATION CHECK™

Photo claims:

Paris.

Could it actually be elsewhere?

Use available:

Landmarks.

Signs.

Metadata where legitimately available.

Weather.

Geographic clues.

But communicate:

CONFIDENCE — NOT FALSE CERTAINTY.

🔥🔥🔥

⏳ TOO OLD™

Information may have been correct:

Five years ago.

Not today.

GottaCheck flags:

Outdated statistics.

Old policies.

Expired offers.

Changed executives.

Superseded research.

TRUE ONCE DOESN'T MEAN TRUE NOW.

🔥🔥🔥

🔄 CHECK AGAIN™

Evidence changes.

New study.

Correction.

Updated filing.

New statement.

Resolved investigation.

Let users revisit:

THE SAME CHECK OVER TIME.

🔥🔥🔥

👀 WATCH THIS™

Important claim unresolved?

Follow it.

GottaCheck alerts when:

New evidence appears.

Source updates.

Correction issued.

Claim resolved.

A check becomes:

A LIVING INVESTIGATION.

🔥🔥🔥

🧾 CHECK RECEIPT™

Every check can produce a concise record:

What was checked.

When.

Sources.

Evidence.

Unknowns.

Risk signals.

Conclusion boundaries.

Share:

THE EVIDENCE — NOT JUST THE VERDICT.

🔥🔥🔥

🚦 CHECK STATUS™

Instead of forcing everything into:

TRUE.

FALSE.

Use more useful states:

Supported.

Contradicted.

Partially supported.

Missing context.

Unverified.

Outdated.

Disputed.

Opinion.

Prediction.

Insufficient evidence.

Because reality rarely fits:

TWO BUTTONS.

🔥🔥🔥

❓ UNKNOWN™

Sometimes the correct answer is:

WE DON'T KNOW YET.

That isn't failure.

It's intellectual honesty.

A trust product becomes more credible when it can say:

INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE.

🔥🔥🔥

⚖️ SHOW BOTH SIDES™

When credible evidence conflicts:

Show it.

Source A.

Source B.

Methodology.

Difference.

Uncertainty.

Users deserve:

THE DISAGREEMENT ITSELF.

🔥🔥🔥

🧭 WHAT NEXT?™

A verification product should end with:

Action.

Example:

Call the company using the number on its official website.

Check the original filing.

Wait for additional confirmation.

Don't send payment yet.

Ask the seller for documentation.

Contact your bank.

The goal isn't merely:

KNOWING MORE.

It's:

MAKING A BETTER NEXT MOVE.

Domain.

Payment.

Urgency.

Link.

Behavior.

Here is V2 of my company "Initiation Report" Deep Research Prompt. Serious thanks to the community for the feedback. This thing is pretty badass now. 
_____
I've made several updates:
• No longer too positive: People rightfully called out that the previous model rated everything a buy. I made several updates. I hardcoded some default investment hurdles (you can change them). But you can see this in action with Shopify, which the new prompt rated a hold (previously it was a buy)

• Entry Points Matter: It now uses the hardcoded investment hurdles to determine the right entry point.

• Business Quality Scorecard: I added a scorecard on business quality. This exists outside valuation. Weights are - Market 25 | Moat 25 | Unit Economics 20 | Execution 15 | Financial Quality 15. Below a 70% and the model rates it a sell. 

• Deeper Analysis: I included six new sections: Ecosystem & Platform Health, Capital Structure & Cost of Capital, Pricing Power & Elasticity Testing, Data & AI Economics – data rights, training-cost curve, AI ROI, Supply Chain & Operations, M&A Strategy & Optionality

• Source Threshold: I tried to code the prompt to require ChatGPT to review at least 60 sources. It works sometimes, but not always

________________
ROLE AND OBJECTIVE
You are a senior buy-side equity analyst with a risk-manager mindset and forensic-accounting rigor.
Produce a decision-ready, source-backed investment memo on {COMPANY_NAME} ({TICKER}) that concludes with a clear Buy / Hold / Sell call.

MINDSET AND APPROACH
• Begin with the outside view, then layer the inside view, deliberately hunting for disconfirming
evidence before trusting the company narrative.
• Lead with downside: map bear paths, covenant or liquidity traps, and execution bottlenecks
before outlining upside drivers.
• Enforce valuation-and-timing discipline by applying hard gates before any rating or position
sizing.
• Show the math—ranges, sensitivities, units, and explicit assumptions—whenever you estimate.

STANDARDS AND CONSTRAINTS
• Finish the Research-coverage standards (60-source gate) *before* drafting any part of the memo.
• Tag every paragraph **Fact / Analysis / Inference** and include unit conversions and
calculations where relevant.
• **Expand acronyms on first use** (e.g., Free Cash Flow (FCF)), then use the acronym
consistently.
• Follow the Decision rules, Quality scorecard, and Entry-readiness overlay exactly as written.

VOICE AND OUTPUTS
• **Start the memo with the Executive summary**—it appears first, ahead of all other sections.
• Write concisely in a structured, neutral style: bullets, tables, and step-by-step math over
long prose.
• The Executive summary must state rating, fair-value band, expected total return, buy/trim
bands, dated catalysts, and “what would change the call.”

PROHIBITIONS
• Never present unsourced assertions as facts or hide uncertainty by omitting known limitations
or error bars.

DEFAULT INVESTMENT HURDLES
(Apply automatically—do not ask the user.)
Metric | Default | Purpose | 
- Decision horizon: 24 months, Scenario & catalyst window
- Benchmark / alpha: S&P 500 / +300 bps, Required out-performance
- Expected-return hurdle: 30 % over 24 m, Minimum probability-weighted total return for Buy
- Margin of safety: 25 %, Required discount to mid fair value
- Return ÷ bear-drawdown skew: ≥ 1.7×, Pay-off asymmetry gate
- Quality pass / sell floor: 70 / 60, Weighted business-quality score

RULES FOR RESEARCH AND WRITING
• Use verifiable sources; date every non-obvious claim so provenance is clear.
• Label paragraphs Fact / Analysis / Inference.
• Use exact calendar dates—avoid “recently” or “last quarter.”
• Quantify material statements; show math and units.
• Highlight missing data and state explicit assumptions.

RESEARCH-COVERAGE & CITATION STANDARDS  (single-run workflow)
1. Internally gather sources; build the Coverage log & Coverage validator.
2. When **all validator lines are PASS**, draft the memo immediately and append the
Coverage log + validator at the end.
• *Coverage log* columns: Title | Link | Date | Source type (filing / earnings-IR /
industry-trade / high-quality media / competitor-primary / academic-expert) | Region |
Domain | Section | Note | Recency Yes/No.
• Count uniqueness by **domain + document title**.
• *PASS thresholds*: ≥ 60 unique sources, ≥ 10 HQ media, ≥ 5 competitor-primary, ≥ 5
academic/expert, ≥ 60 % dated within 24 months, ≤ 10 % from any one domain.
• Mark *Recency Yes* for each time-sensitive metric; print its date; update if newer data
exist or justify retention.
• If any validator line is FAIL, keep researching silently until all PASS; **never prompt the
user after validation**.

DECISION RULES FOR RATING AND ENTRY (single source of truth)
1. Compute expected total return
E[TR] = p_bull·R_bull + p_base·R_base + p_bear·R_bear (dividends + buybacks).
2. Quantify downside: bear-case total return, expected shortfall, maximum adverse excursion.
3. **Margin-of-safety gate:** Price ≥ {MOS_%} below intrinsic value **unless** a near-certain
≤ 6-month catalyst with quantified impact and ≥ 80 % probability (cited) offsets it.
4. **Skew gate:** E[TR] ÷ |bear-drawdown| ≥ {SKEW_X}.
5. **Why-now gate:** Require a dated catalyst or re-rating trigger inside {HORIZON}; else
Hold / Wait-for-entry.
6. Provide buy / hold / trim bands around fair value and explicit add/reduce rules.
7. If any gate fails → rating cannot be **Buy**; assign Hold, Wait-for-entry, or Sell.

QUALITY SCORECARD
• Weights: Market 25 | Moat 25 | Unit Economics 20 | Execution 15 | Financial Quality 15.
• Score each 0–5 (evidence for >3); weighted total = Quality score.
• Buy if Quality ≥ {QUALITY_PASS} **and** all gates pass; Sell if Quality < {QUALITY_SELL}.
• Output the five subscores and the total.
ENTRY READINESS OVERLAY
• Derive posture (Strong Buy / Buy / Watch / Trim) from Decision-rule outputs; header:
“Quality = XX/100 | Entry = …”.

DELIVERABLES (order)
1. Executive summary (first)
2. Full memo (Sections 1–21)
3. Coverage log + Coverage validator
4. Appendix (model, data tables, assumptions)

OUTPUT SEQUENCE
Executive summary → Rating & price targets → Investment thesis & variant perception → Decision
rules / Quality scorecard / Entry overlay → Sections 1–21 → Coverage log + validator →
Appendix.

SECTIONS 1 – 21  (fully descriptive one-sentence bullets)

1) THESIS FRAMING (purpose – define what must be true to create value)
• Summarize in one crisp question the value-creation hurdle the investment must clear.
• State 3–5 thesis pillars, each as a concrete “if-then” condition linking business drivers to
shareholder value.
• List the specific facts that would disprove each pillar so falsification is easy.
• Give a dated, single-sentence “why-now” catalyst that explains timing.
• Explain the variant perception—the edge versus consensus and why the market misses it.
• Name the leading metric and break-point threshold that would invalidate the thesis within two quarters.

2) MARKET STRUCTURE AND SIZE (purpose – size the prize and trajectory)
• Quantify Total, Serviceable, and Share-of-Market by product line, customer band, industry,
and geography so upside is tangible.
• Tie each major growth driver (regulation, refresh cycles, macro, tech adoption) to a
quantifiable lift in demand.
• Benchmark current penetration versus peer adoption curves to measure runway.
• Spell out scenarios that could shrink Serviceable TAM in the next 24 months.
• State clearly whether demand or supply is the binding constraint today and cite evidence.

3) CUSTOMER SEGMENTS AND JOBS (purpose – map who buys and why)
• Break down the customer mix by size band and industry and name buyer roles and budget
owners.
• Map core workflows, pain points, and mission-criticality to show value dependency.
• Quantify switching costs for each segment to gauge durability.
• Estimate do-nothing/internal-build prevalence and why customers still convert.
• Identify the main procurement blocker and the proof required to unlock purchase.

4) PRODUCT AND ROADMAP (purpose – evaluate product-market fit and durability)
• List core modules and adjacencies and tie differentiators to measurable user outcomes.
• Compare depth versus breadth against best-of-breed point solutions to highlight edge.
• State typical implementation time, integrations required, configurability, and
time-to-value.
• Provide quality signals—uptime %, incident frequency, mobile performance—benchmarking
peers.
• Score roadmap credibility by matching stated milestones to historical delivery.
• Highlight the hardest-to-copy capability and the moat protecting it (IP, data, process).
• Flag technical debt that limits scale, reliability, or unit cost within two years.

5) COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE (purpose – position the company)
• Chart direct and indirect competitors by segment and size to show buyer choice set.
• Compare pricing, packaging, and feature gaps, including switching friction and contract
terms.
• Summarize win/loss reasons from reviews, case studies, and disclosed data to evidence edge.
• Anticipate competitor responses and what could neutralize current advantages.
• Flag segments won mainly via channel or regulation rather than product and assess
durability.

6) ECOSYSTEM AND PLATFORM HEALTH (purpose – flywheel durability)
• Report API call volume, active developers/apps, SDK adoption, deprecation cadence, and
backward-compatibility discipline to gauge platform vitality.
• Quantify marketplace economics—GMV, take-rate, rev-share, partner attach, concentration,
leakage control—to show ecosystem value capture.
• Rate partner quality through certifications, pipeline influence, co-sell productivity, and retention or satisfaction scores.
• Detail governance and trust mechanics: listing standards, review SLAs, enforcement, data
sharing, dispute resolution—showing rule-of-law strength.
• Evaluate developer experience via docs quality, sandbox speed, time-to-first-call, and
frequency of breaking changes.
• Define a minimum-viable ecosystem health metric and describe its failure modes.
• State ecosystem-mediated revenue share and any top-partner concentration risk.

7) GO-TO-MARKET AND DISTRIBUTION (purpose – scalability of new-logo engine)
• Break down demand sources (inbound, outbound, partner referral, marketplaces) and show
historical mix shift.
• Quantify sales productivity—ramp duration, quota attainment %, conversion rates—and link
to disclosed or inferred data.
• Explain channel and partnership roles (integrations, OEM, platform embeds) in extending
reach.
• Describe services and customer-success motions and how training/community become moat.
• Name the single biggest funnel bottleneck and the lowest-CAC play to clear it.
• Specify what doubling pipeline without doubling opex would require in headcount, spend, or
tooling.

8) RETENTION AND EXPANSION (purpose – revenue durability)
• Report gross and net dollar retention by cohort and segment or provide transparent
estimation math.
• Diagnose logo churn drivers and timing; visualise a churn curve if shape matters.
• List expansion vectors—seat growth, module attach, usage add-ons—and rank by revenue
impact.
• Detail contract length, renewal mechanics, and price-increase policies to gauge stickiness.
• Synthesize reference-call insights or credible reviews to validate retention claims.
• Identify a leading churn indicator 60–90 days ahead and show how it triggers action.
• Split expansion into true usage growth versus price/packaging uplift by cohort.

9) MONETIZATION MODEL AND REVENUE QUALITY (purpose – value capture → durable revenue)
• Map revenue architecture by model (subscription, license, usage, transaction, hardware,
services, advertising, marketplace) and state the revenue *unit* for each line.
• Identify price meters and prove they correlate with delivered customer value.
• Show gross and contribution margin by line and sensitivity to mix shift.
• Describe revenue recognition policy, seasonality patterns, and the roles of bookings,
backlog, and Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO).
• Quantify visibility—contracted, recurring, re-occurring, non-recurring—and concentration
by customer, product, channel, geography.
• Explain external demand drivers (macro cycles, ad markets, commodity inputs, interest-rate
sensitivity, regulatory constraints) that can swing volumes.
• List 2–3 leading KPIs per model that predict revenue one to two quarters ahead and show
empirical lead-lag.
• If payments/credit apply, add activity levels, take rate, cost stack, loss rates, and who bears credit/fraud risk.
• Identify the price meter best aligned with value that can scale 10× without raising churn.
• Flag any revenue line that carries negative optionality or cannibalizes a higher-margin
line.

10) PRICING POWER AND ELASTICITY TESTING (purpose – value capture)
• Document pricing governance—list vs realized price history, discount band discipline,
approval thresholds, and price fences.
• Present elasticity evidence from controlled price tests, cohort outcomes, win/loss data,
and cross-price effects.
• Summarize willingness-to-pay research (conjoint or van Westendorp), key buyer value
drivers, and sensitivity by industry/size.
• Explain packaging strategy—good-better-best tiers, bundle attach, usage/overage meters—and
leakage guardrails.
• Provide a monetization-change log of pricing/packaging/metering moves and realized impact.
• State reference price and switching cost (dollars/hours) by segment to ground barriers.
• Estimate ARPU ceiling before churn inflects and cite supporting evidence.

11) UNIT ECONOMICS AND EFFICIENCY (purpose – profitable scalability)
• Report CAC, payback period, magic number, and LTV/CAC by segment—stated or transparently inferred.
• Show contribution margin by line (software, usage, services) to reveal variable profit.
• Track cohort profitability and cumulative cash contribution over time to evidence
unit-level returns.
• Quantify implementation, onboarding, and support cost over lifetime to fully load
economics.
• Identify structurally unprofitable cohorts and whether strategy is fix or exit.
• Name the main constraint blocking a 20–30 % payback improvement and the remedy.
12) FINANCIAL PROFILE (purpose – operations → financial outcomes)
• Break down revenue mix and growth by component and gross margin by line, then show the
operating-leverage path.
• Present Rule-of-40 score and a GAAP-to-cash-flow bridge to reconcile accounting with liquidity.
• Highlight leading indicators (billings, RPO, backlog) that foreshadow revenue.
• Detail stock-based-compensation, dilution, and share-count trajectory.
• Explain liquidity needs, working-capital profile, and path to FCF breakeven and target
margin.
• State operational milestones required to hit target FCF margin and timeline.
• Flag accounting judgments that could swing EBIT by > 200 bps and show sensitivity.
• Compute the FCF/share CAGR needed to reach mid fair value and assess feasibility.
13) CAPITAL STRUCTURE AND COST OF CAPITAL (purpose – funding flexibility and risk)
• Detail the debt stack—instrument types, fixed/floating mix, hedges, covenants, collateral, maturities, amortization, prepay terms—to surface refinancing risk.
• Quantify leverage and coverage (gross/net, interest-coverage, Debt/EBITDA vs covenant
headroom) and stress for higher rates and lower EBITDA.
• Estimate WACC—capital-structure weights, risk-free rate, beta, equity risk premium,
credit spread—and show sensitivities.
• Summarize rating-agency posture and triggers and compare to management targets.
• Map equity plumbing—authorized vs issued, converts, buybacks, dividend policy, ATM,
option/RSU overhang—to project dilution.
• Identify funding shock or rate level that forces a strategy shift or covenant breach and
outline the contingency plan.
• State headroom to fund growth at target leverage while preserving ratings.
• Define liquidity runway and covenant headroom thresholds that force Sell or Wait.

14) MOAT AND DATA ADVANTAGE (purpose – defensibility)
• Explain workflow depth and proprietary data that create lock-in.
• Analyze network or ecosystem effects, showing how value strengthens with scale.
• Demonstrate measurable analytics or AI advantages that translate to outcomes.
• Map integration footprint and practical switching costs across adjacent systems.
• Provide evidence the moat is deepening over time, not static or eroding.
• Identify the event most likely to collapse the moat within two years and estimate its
probability.

15) DATA AND ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE ECONOMICS (purpose – margin drivers)
• Describe data sources, ownership rights, exclusivity, consent provenance, refresh cadence,
and quality controls that underpin AI.
• Quantify labeling/curation costs, model-training compute, per-inference cost, and
unit-cost decline roadmap.
• Assess vendor and IP risk—model or infrastructure dependencies, portability, open-/closed-source posture, patent coverage, and freedom-to-operate.
• Outline evaluation framework—offline/online tests, attributable KPIs, guardrails,
drift-detection, rollback policies—to ensure model quality.
• Evaluate data-moat mechanics—uniqueness, scale, timeliness, feedback loops—separate from
general network effects.
• Describe the self-reinforcing data loop and contractual protection for
rights/consent/exclusivity.
• Estimate marginal ROI of each AI feature versus a non-AI baseline and how ROI scales.

16) EXECUTION QUALITY AND ORGANIZATION (purpose – operating cadence)
• Summarize leadership track record, stability, organizational design, and succession
readiness.
• Report engineering velocity—release cadence, defect and incident rates—where data exist.
• Triangulate customer sentiment using CSAT, NPS, peer reviews, and community signals.
• Flag a single leadership gap that is existential within 12–24 months and outline the
succession or hire plan.
• Name the operating-cadence metric that best predicts misses and describe how it triggers
action.

17) SUPPLY CHAIN AND OPERATIONS (purpose – fulfilment and cost risk; include if
hardware/services heavy)
• List critical suppliers, single-source exposures, top-5 concentration, capacity
commitments, lead times, yields, and quality escapes.
• Provide field performance—warranty accruals vs claims, RMA rates/roots, refurbishment recovery, inventory turns, aging, and obsolescence reserves.
• Describe logistics/continuity—key lanes, 3PL dependencies, regional diversification,
tariff/export-control exposure, dual-sourcing and disaster-recovery plans.
• Explain manufacturing economics—make-vs-buy logic, contract-manufacturer terms,
learning-curve slope, utilization breakevens.
• If services are material, show staffing levels, utilization, backlog, SLA attainment, and
margin by tier.
• Identify the single point of failure and quantify time/cost to dual-source it.
• Compare cost-curve and yield learning rate versus peers and note what would change the slope.

18) RISK INVENTORY AND MITIGANTS (purpose – make downside explicit)
• Prioritize macro, regulatory, competitive, operational, and concentration risks with plain
impact descriptions.
• Include payments, credit, or compliance risks if the model warrants.
• Highlight implementation complexity and time-to-value risk with realistic timelines.
• Lead with indicators and mitigations; cross-reference covenant/liquidity metrics (Section 13)
and supply-chain continuity (Section 17).
• Name the top 12-month risk, quantify P&L impact, and outline a recovery playbook.
• Define an objective stop-loss or escalation trigger that forces capital preservation.

19) MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS STRATEGY AND OPTIONALITY (purpose – non-organic growth)
• Review past deals versus plan—revenue, margin, cash-flow, synergy capture, post-merger
churn, integration cost.
• Apply a build-buy-partner framework to close roadmap gaps with evidence.
• Assess integration muscle—playbooks, platform convergence, leadership retention, cultural integration, systems/process harmonization.
• Summarize financing mix, valuation discipline versus comps, earn-outs/contingent
consideration, and impairment history.
• Describe M&A pipeline, regulatory environment, and how acquisitions shift competitive
dynamics and thesis risk.
• Identify capability gaps that cannot be built organically in time and why acquisition is
needed.

20) VALUATION FRAMEWORK (purpose – value with cross-checks)
• Establish an outside-view baseline using peer medians/IQR for growth, margins, reinvestment, and valuation; justify deviations.
• Present a public-comps table—growth, gross margin, operating margin, Rule-of-40,
EV/Revenue, EV/Gross Profit—normalized for disclosure quirks.
• Build a discounted-cash-flow (DCF) with explicit drivers and sensitivity bands to show
value swing.
• Run a reverse-DCF to surface market-implied growth, margins, reinvestment and explain
where you disagree.
• Output a fair-value band (low/mid/high) and required {MOS_%} margin-of-safety to act.
• Benchmark current multiple versus 5-year peer percentile and only recommend Buy if a
credible re-rating path exists.
• Cross-check value with cohort NPV math, adoption S-curves, and unit-economics-to-EV sanity
checks.
• For private names, triangulate valuation using last-round terms, secondary indications,
and revenue multiples.
• State market-implied expectations from the reverse-DCF and the single variable explaining
most dispersion.

21) SCENARIOS, CATALYSTS, AND MONITORING PLAN (purpose – expectations and triggers)
• Build 12–24 month bear, base, and bull cases—NRR, new-logo adds, pricing/take rate,
margins, SBC, share count—with probabilities summing to 100 %.
• Compute probability-weighted E[TR] and block Buy if below {HURDLE_TR_%}.
• Lead with bear path: bear price/drawdown, recovery path, and time to recoup.
• Perform a reverse stress test with hard triggers, a stress price band, and
pre-committed downgrade/re-entry rules.
• List near-term catalysts with firm dates and quantified impact on key numbers or multiple.
• Provide an entry plan with buy/add/trim/exit bands tied to price and thesis-break metrics.
• Monitor early warnings—small-cohort churn spikes, backlog slippage, uptime incidents,
pricing pushback—with clear symptom → action mapping.
• Define stop/review levels when metrics breach or price hits bear band without catalyst
progress.
• Rank expected return per unit downside versus two realistic alternatives to surface opportunity cost.
• End with three positive and three negative “change-my-mind” triggers that would flip the
rating.

MODELING INSTRUCTIONS (simple but defensible)
• Build revenue by segment/product; if usage-based, include volume & take-rate drivers.
• Estimate gross margin by line; set operating-expense ratios and SBC; output free-cash-flow.
• Provide share-count & dilution schedule for the next eight quarters (public names).
• Include two-way sensitivity tables on the two most material drivers.
• Reconcile GAAP operating loss to FCF with a clear bridge.
RATING LOGIC — assign Buy / Hold / Wait-for-entry / Sell strictly per Decision rules.
QUALITY BAR — back key statements with numbers & citations; label speculation **Inference**;
prefer bullets & tables; keep prose tight.

ECI’S NEW SIR ORDERS: A COURSE CORRECTION — OR A RESPONSE TO THE QUESTIONS?

The Election Commission’s latest press note introduces several important changes to the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process.

Most significantly, voters who receive notices for being “unmapped” or having “logical discrepancies” will no longer ordinarily be required to appear personally before the ERO. Booth Level Officers (BLOs) will visit their homes, collect documents and upload them on ECINet. Hearings will be held only in exceptional circumstances, preferably online. 

The Commission has also directed District Election Officers to establish help desks and special camps for night-shelter residents, labourers, poor and homeless citizens—groups for whom documentation and physical appearances can create particular difficulties.

Another significant decision is the extension of the claims-and-objections period in Delhi up to 30 October 2026, with disposal extended to 30 November. Maharashtra has also received an extension, with claims and objections permitted until 12 October and disposal until 10 November, according to the Commission’s press note.

The ECI has further announced an independent expert review of ECINet, involving an expert from IIT/IIM, to examine whether the system complies with the relevant Acts and Rules.

But the timing is important.

Just days earlier, The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally raised objections on at least 14 occasions concerning aspects of the SIR process, including voter additions/deletions and access to electoral data. 

The Election Commission has rejected the characterization of these differences as institutional dissent, maintaining that final decisions—including SIR—were taken unanimously by the full Commission. The 26 September press note reiterates that position. 

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court, during proceedings on Delhi SIR on 22 September, questioned the process by which “logical discrepancy” notices were being generated and asked the ECI to consider additional safeguards and clearer guidance for affected voters. 

So the real issue is not simply whether the ECI has changed its procedure.

It is whether these changes will make the process more transparent, accessible and demonstrably protective of every eligible voter’s right to remain on the electoral roll.

A notice should not become a barrier to voting.
A software-generated discrepancy should not become a substitute for human verification.
And every eligible citizen must have a meaningful opportunity to establish their right to vote.

The credibility of SIR will ultimately depend not merely on the number of names added or removed, but on whether every eligible voter can understand, challenge and correct the process affecting their franchise.

Source: Election Commission of India Press Note No. ECI/PN/120/2026, dated 26 September 2026.

Today, I joined the protest organised by the Karnataka Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC) at Freedom Park against the functioning of the Election Commission of India, as part of the nationwide agitation led by the Congress demanding the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

In Karnataka, the protest is being held under the leadership of KPCC President B.K. Hariprasad, with various political parties and organisations participating in support of Shri Rahul Gandhi’s struggle to protect our democracy.

The recent developments within the Election Commission and the manner in which it is functioning have caused serious concern among everyone who believes in democracy.

The Election Commission is a constitutional institution. Its duty is to conduct elections independently, impartially and transparently, in accordance with the spirit of our Constitution. Free and fair elections are the foundation of democracy. If the Election Commission loses its independence, democracy itself cannot survive. This is a question of the very survival of our democracy.

If members of the Election Commission are found to have acted against the Constitution, constitutional action must follow. The Hon’ble President of India, who has a responsibility to safeguard the Constitution, must intervene. Neither the Chief Election Commissioner nor any Election Commissioner has the constitutional authority to function in an authoritarian manner.

The Election Commission owes allegiance neither to a government nor to a political party. Its allegiance must be only to the Constitution given to us by Babasaheb Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. It cannot be reduced to an institution that functions to the tune of the Union Government.

The Election Commission currently has three members, including the Chief Election Commissioner. Media reports, however, have revealed that the other two Election Commissioners have repeatedly recorded written objections to several decisions.

According to an investigative report, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi have raised objections on at least 14 occasions over the past 10 months to decisions and orders of the Commission. When two members of a three-member constitutional body themselves repeatedly raise objections, it is an extremely serious matter. Such developments should never arise within an institution entrusted with protecting the integrity of our elections.

The Election Commission’s core responsibilities include revising electoral rolls, registering new voters, including eligible citizens, removing ineligible names and maintaining electoral data. Above all, it must ensure that elections are conducted lawfully and fairly.
